refuted_claims: The ratchet figure lives in FIVE places and the first version moved two. The cargo shim in the gate's own falsification suite carried a canned '43 ignored' and gate F went red inside its own tests; the new invariant caught that. Review then found two more, in crates/forjar-contracts/Cargo.toml and VENDORED.md. Lane 2 asserted, measured, that nothing was left behind anywhere, and was wrong; lanes 1 and 3 each found sites the other missed. One of lane 3's two is a completed roadmap row whose title records what was true when filed and stays as filed.
The suite shipped an attribute parser whose output was discarded — a leftover from a rule already replaced. All three lanes found it. Removed rather than wired up.

The sibling-check rule was evadable by moving the check one call deep, and cross_project_tests.rs was passing it by exactly that accident rather than by decision. The scan is file-wide now and that file is exempt BY NAME with its reason, with a case that fails if the exemption stops applying. Measured: a helper-hidden version in a non-exempt file is caught now and was not before. The docstring, which had claimed semantic awareness it does not have, now says it is a text ratchet and names what it cannot catch.

crux.verdict: all three surveyed systems make the question disappear rather than answer it: cargo vendor and Go's vendor/ exclude vendored tests from the run entirely, and Debian packaging disables what it cannot run but records only the decision, not a count. forjar is stricter than all three — the tests still compile and run every build, each names its own reason, and the count is ratcheted EXACTLY in both directions. The cost of being stricter is that an exact figure living in five places rots unless something checks it, and nothing did; this ticket adds that check. None of the three has a notion of a test that decides whether to assert by looking at what else is on the disk, which is the defect removed here.
